title: The Apostolic Fathers
altTitles: The Apostolic Fathers with Justin Martyr and Irenaeus
attributionNote: The Apostolic Fathers is a modern collection, not a single book: Clement of Rome's letter to the Corinthians, the letter to Diognetus, Polycarp's letter to the Philippians and the account of his martyrdom, the seven letters of Ignatius of Antioch, the letter of Barnabas and the fragments of Papias. Their authors are named by the manuscripts and the tradition, and the collection itself was assembled by 17th-century editors.
description: The Apostolic Fathers are the Christian writings closest to the New Testament: a letter from the church of Rome to Corinth written before the end of the first century, the letters Ignatius wrote on his way to martyrdom at Rome, Polycarp's instructions to a divided congregation and the eyewitness account of his death, the allegorical letter of Barnabas, the apologetic address to Diognetus, and the fragments of Papias on the origins of the Gospels. They show the churches finding their institutions, their creeds and their relation to Judaism in the generation after the apostles.
historicalContext: The collection stands between the apostolic age and the great patristic writers. Clement writes in the aftermath of a Corinthian quarrel, Ignatius in the last weeks of his life under Trajan, and Papias records traditions about Mark and Matthew that the later church preserved. The texts are translated in the Ante-Nicene Fathers, the 1885 Edinburgh series edited by Alexander Roberts and James Donaldson, from the Greek except where only a Latin or Syriac version survives.
availabilityNote: The archive's transcription of the Apostolic Fathers is complete for the documents it carries: 1 Clement, Diognetus, Polycarp, the Martyrdom of Polycarp, the seven letters of Ignatius, Barnabas and the fragments of Papias, read as one continuous outline with each document prefixed to its chapter labels. Two omissions are the source's: 2 Clement is not in this transcription, and the Syriac recensions and the spurious Ignatian letters printed later in the volume are not included here. Each Ignatian chapter prints the shorter and the longer Latin recension together, as the printed volume does.
